title: Chronicles beside Samuel and Kings
lead: About half of 1 and 2 Chronicles runs parallel to Samuel and Kings, often word for word. Comparing the two accounts shows what Chronicles kept, changed, added and left out, and the comparison has shaped every modern view of how the Bible's histories were written and copied.

sections.b: Chronicles retells Israel's story from Saul's death (1 Chronicles 10, from 1 Samuel 31) to the fall of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 36, from 2 Kings 24–25). Long stretches are copied closely: David's capture of Jerusalem, the ark, Nathan's oracle, David's wars, the census, Solomon's Temple and prayer, and the reigns of Judah's kings. It also borrows from Genesis for its genealogies and from the Psalms for David's song (1 Chronicles 16:8–36). Where the two accounts agree word for word, they are like two copies of one text, and where they differ, the difference is usually meaningful.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:1–14; 1 Samuel 31:1–13; 1 Chronicles 17:1–27; 2 Samuel 7:1–29; 2 Chronicles 6:1–42; 1 Kings 8:12–53

sections.b: 1. Chronicles' own changes. The Chronicler leaves out David's years in Hebron, Bathsheba, Absalom's revolt and Solomon's foreign wives, and adds the Levites, the singers and David's Temple plans. He explains Uzzah's death and Saul's fall in his own words (1 Chronicles 13:10; 10:13–14). 2. A different Samuel text. The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a and the Greek of Samuel often agree with Chronicles against the Masoretic Samuel (Baalah, 2 Samuel 6:2; the thousand chariots, 2 Samuel 8:4). So Chronicles sometimes preserves an older Samuel than the one in our Hebrew Bibles. 3. Copying slips. Lists of names and numbers drift in both books, as when an eye skips from one repeated phrase to the next (1 Chronicles 11:13).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 13:10; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14; 2 Samuel 6:2; 2 Samuel 8:4; 1 Chronicles 11:13; 1 Chronicles 18:4

sections.b: Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, have read Chronicles as a second inspired history that supplements Kings (its Greek name, Paraleipomena, means "things left out") and names its own sources, such as the records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29). Nineteenth-century critics such as Julius Wellhausen judged Chronicles a late, idealizing rewrite of little historical value. Most scholars today take a middle view: Chronicles is a theological history for the community after the exile, written with clear aims, that still preserves some older material and good textual readings. Scholars such as Sara Japhet, H. G. M. Williamson and Gary Knoppers have shown how closely its changes follow a consistent theology. A minority (A. Graeme Auld) argues that Samuel–Kings and Chronicles both drew on a shared older story.
